name: Mirror equation
seoDesc: Mirror equation: work out object distance (−) from the image distance and the focal length. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked…
summary: Supply the image distance, the focal length, the radius of curvature and the linear magnification and the Mirror equation calculator solves for object distance (−). That makes it useful for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Mirror equation calculator work?
sections.html:
The Mirror equation calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports object distance (−) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the mirror type); then you type in the image distance (+/−), the focal length (−), the radius of curvature (+) and the linear magnification (+).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Mirror equation calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Object distance (−)=-focal length (−) × image distance (+ ÷ −) ÷ (focal length (−) − image distance (+ ÷ −))
Radius of curvature (−)=2 × focal length (−)
Object distance (−)=-image distance (+ ÷ −) ÷ linear magnification (+ ÷ −)
Object distance (−)=image distance (+ ÷ −) × the square root of (1 ÷ areal magnification (+))
Image distance (+)=-focal length (+) × object distance (−) ÷ (focal length (+) − object distance (−))
Focal length (+)=(1 ÷ 2) × radius of curvature (+)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Mirror type set to Concave mirror, Image distance (+/−) = 30 cm and Focal length (−) = 30 cm. The calculator returns Radius of curvature (−) = 60 cm.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Radius of curvature (−) = 60 cm should be roughly the size you expected from Mirror type set to Concave mirror and Image distance (+/−) = 30 cm.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Mirror equation calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the image distance, the focal length and the radius of curvature — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Mirror equation calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns object distance (−), derived from the image distance, the focal length and the radius of curvature. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Mirror equation calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the image distance, the focal length, the radius of curvature and the linear magnification, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter object distance (−) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Object distance (−) opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Radius of curvature (−) = 60 cm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Mirror equation calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
